text: The term \((E[X])^2\operatorname{Var}(N)\) is the part of \(\operatorname{Var}(S)\) that comes from not knowing how many summands there will be. Omitting it is correct only when the term genuinely vanishes: when \(\mu=0\), or when \(N\) is almost surely constant so that \(\operatorname{Var}(N)=0\). The formula also requires \(N\) to be independent of every \(X_i\). If \(N\) is a stopping time built from the \(X_i\), the conditional law of the summands given \(N=n\) is no longer the original i.i.d. law, and the conditional identities \(E[S\mid N=n]=n\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N=n)=n\sigma^2\) can fail. The mean formula \(E[S]=E[N]\mu\) still holds when \(E[N]\) and \(E[|X_1|]\) are finite (Wald's equation), but the variance formula can fail: for steps of 1 or 2 with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, stopped once the total reaches 2, the formula gives \(\tfrac{15}{16}\) while the true variance is \(\tfrac{3}{16}\). Finally \(E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]\) is a number, whereas \(\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)\) is a random variable.
